title: A scarlet cosmic sea
caption: Part of the Gum 10 nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A sea of scarlet gas, broken by dark patches, fills this view of part of the Gum 10 nebula in the constellation Puppis, seen through ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The colour has a clear cause. Hot blue stars inside Gum 10 pour out energetic ultraviolet radiation that ionises the nebula's gas, stripping electrons from their atoms. When the electrons rejoin the atoms, they give off light at very particular colours. In Gum 10 the red is the signature of hydrogen, which is more plentiful than any other element in the Universe.

Darker patches mark thick clouds of dust that partly block our view of whatever lies behind them. The nebula takes its name from the Australian astronomer Colin Stanley Gum, who discovered it and in 1955 published a catalogue of more than 80 similar diffuse nebulae.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through b, v and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
filters: 440 nm · Optical b (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
557 nm · Optical v (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
655 nm · Optical R (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
656 nm · Optical H-alpha (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures bring out a red glow that would be very faint to the eye.

explore: The image was taken with the FORS2 instrument as part of ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time that cannot be used for science to make outreach images. The data are also made available to astronomers through ESO's science archive.
alt: Scarlet glowing gas with dark patches of dust and scattered stars.
